units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, quick quiz. When was Luxembourg born?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Depends who you ask. Some say 1815, when the Grand Duchy was created at the Congress of Vienna.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Others say 1839, when its modern borders were drawn in London.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Others point to 1867, when the great powers guaranteed its independence.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But you have your own answer.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: I do. The story really starts in the year nine sixty-three, with a land swap.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A land swap. That's the founding moment.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Not a battle, not a coronation.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Not a sword in sight.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Disappointing. I'd have bet on a sword.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You'd have lost. But before the land swap, there's a man we have to meet.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He has no name. Archaeologists call him Loschbour man, after the rock shelter near the village of Heffingen where his skeleton was found in 1935.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He lived about eight thousand years ago, when this land was dense forest and people survived by hunting, fishing, and gathering.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And he made headlines.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Decades after his discovery, scientists sequenced his DNA.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The result suggested that this early European had dark skin and blue eyes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Huh. That's not the picture most of us have in our heads.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It overturned a lot of assumptions about what the first Europeans looked like.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who came next?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Farmers, from the southeast. They cleared fields along the river valleys.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then the age of metal, first bronze and later iron.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the last centuries before Christ, the land of Luxembourg belonged to a Celtic people called the Treveri.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who left something behind.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A fortified hilltop town called the Titelberg, in the far southwest of today's country, near the French border.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: High plateau, ramparts all around, a center for metalworking and trade, and one of the best cavalry traditions in Gaul.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Cavalry. Of course it was cavalry.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And then Rome arrives.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Naturally.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The first written mention of this land comes from Julius Caesar himself, in his account of the Gallic Wars.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the middle of the first century before Christ, he fought the Treveri.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: After years of rebellion and repression, the region was swallowed into the Roman Empire.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So what did the Romans build?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A city nearby, on the Moselle, just across what's now the German border.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Augusta Treverorum. Today it's called Trier.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Trier. I've heard of Trier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Within a few generations it was one of the great cities of the western empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At one point it was home to emperors, and its Roman gates and baths still stand.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So where does Luxembourg fit in?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's Trier's backyard. Farmland and forest, crossed by Roman roads, and dotted with country estates.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One road ran from Reims, in what's now France, to Trier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Along it, near today's village of Dalheim, a small Roman town grew up, complete with a theater.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A theater, in the backyard of the backyard.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And villas. At Echternach and at Diekirch, wealthy landowners built grand ones.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A Roman mosaic from one of the Diekirch houses survives, laid out in colored stone.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Sounds comfortable.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Settled, Latin-speaking, and for a few centuries, secure.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But it didn't last.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No. In the third and fourth centuries, raiders pushed across the Rhine, and Roman power along the frontier began to wear away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the end of the fifth century the region belonged to the Franks, a Germanic people whose king, Clovis, was building a new kingdom out of the ruins of Roman Gaul.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which brings a new religion.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Through some remarkable missionaries.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The one that matters for us is a monk named Willibrord.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Born in Northumbria, in England, trained in Ireland.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Well traveled.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He crossed the sea to preach to the pagan Frisians, and in the year six ninety-eight he founded a monastery at Echternach, on land given to him by a noblewoman from the Trier area.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He died in seven thirty-nine, and he was buried there.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Echternach became a big deal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the great intellectual centers of medieval Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Its monks copied and illuminated manuscripts so beautiful that they're treasured in museums in Germany today.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's a dance. I've heard there's a dance.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Every year, on the Tuesday after Pentecost, thousands of people dance through the streets of Echternach in honor of Saint Willibrord.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They hop in time to a simple, polka-like tune.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Hop. Thousands of people. In the street.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: UNESCO recognizes it as part of humanity's living cultural heritage.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, that's going on my list.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Now, Charlemagne.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Finally. A name I know.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the late eighth and early ninth centuries, the Frankish kings became emperors, and this region sat comfortably inside their realm.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But when Charlemagne's empire was split among his grandsons by the Treaty of Verdun in eight forty-three, the land that would become Luxembourg fell into the middle kingdom, named after the grandson Lothar.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which didn't last either, did it?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It broke up over the following decades.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The region became a borderland, a long-contested strip between the western Frankish kingdom, which would become France, and the eastern Frankish kingdom, which would become Germany.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So it was born in the middle of an argument.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It was. And in the year nine sixty-two, in Rome, a German king named Otto was crowned emperor.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His realm would later be called the Holy Roman Empire, a loose, shifting collection of kingdoms, duchies, counties and church lands that would last more than eight hundred years.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And one year later?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A count named Siegfried made a small land deal that no one at the time could have thought important.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, who was Siegfried?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He belonged to a noble family from the Moselle and Ardennes region, and according to tradition he had Carolingian blood.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: What he wanted was a stronghold.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the edge of his lands there was a rocky promontory above the river Alzette, with the ruins of an old fortification.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which belonged to someone else.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: To the abbey of Saint Maximin, in Trier.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Siegfried offered other lands in exchange, and the monks said yes.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the founding of Luxembourg is a property swap with monks.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the charter survives. It's dated nine sixty-three, and it names the place: Lucilinburhuc.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: That means, roughly, little castle.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Little castle. Cute.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In time, the name softened and shortened into Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the rock itself?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's known as the Bock. Siegfried built a real fortress on it, and his family spread out from there across the surrounding land.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The spot was so well chosen that armies would fight over it for the next nine hundred years.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I have a feeling there's a legend.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Of course there is. It says Siegfried married a mermaid named Melusina, who agreed to live with him on one condition.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He must never look at her on a certain day.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And he looked.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He looked. She vanished beneath the waters of the Alzette, and left him alone.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Classic.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And locals say she can still be seen, once every seven years, spinning at the bottom of the river.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, I'm choosing to believe that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The real story is even better.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Because from this little rocky outcrop, Siegfried's descendants would rise to the heights of European power.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They'd sit on the throne of Bohemia, and wear the imperial crown.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: From a swap with some monks to an emperor's crown.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: I want to hear about that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Next chapter. We meet the House of Luxembourg.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I'm betting they're a lot of trouble.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Quite a family.
